en: The Tripitaka Master Wuxiang (Sanskrit name: Śubhakarasiṃha;
translated into Chinese as Shàn Wúwèi), of the Kṣatriya caste, a Dhyāna Master from the city of Rājagṛha in Magadha, Central India, at Nālandā Venuvana Monastery. He was a Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa.

The noble and eminent clansman, together with the Great Virtuous Chan Master of Songyue Heshan Temple, Reverend Jingxian, engaged in a discussion on the Buddha-dharma. He briefly set forth the essential tenets of the Mahāyāna to suddenly open the minds of sentient beings so that they might swiftly awaken to the Way, as well as the ritual procedures for the *karmavācanā* of the Bodhisattva precepts; these are recorded in the following sequence.
Now, those who wish to enter the Mahāyāna Dharma must first give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta and receive the great Bodhisattva precepts.
Only when the vessel of the body is purified may they then receive the Dharma.
This is briefly analyzed into eleven sections: first, the section on generating the resolve; second, the section on making offerings;

third, the section on repentance; fourth, the section on taking refuge; fifth, the section on generating the bodhicitta; sixth, the section on inquiring about impediments; seventh, the section on requesting a preceptor; eighth, the section on the *karmavācanā*; ninth, the section on delimiting the boundary; tenth, the section on practicing the four means of attraction; and eleventh, the section on the ten grave precepts.

1. Chapter on Arousing the Bodhicitta, Part One: Chapter on Arousing the Mind. Disciples such as I, [Name], take refuge in the Great Bodhicitta of all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, who act as our great guides, capable of causing us to leave behind all evil realms and capable of showing the path to the Great Nirvana of humans and devas; for this reason, we now prostrate with the utmost sincerity.

2. The Second Gate: Offerings. Next, one should instruct the disciple to direct the mind to visualize all Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the infinite worlds, the oceans of lands as numerous as atoms, and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as many as the sands of the Ganges. One should imagine that before each and every Buddha, the disciple [Name], together with others, prostrates, praises, and makes offerings. All the most excellent, sublime, and wondrous incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and various superior articles throughout the worlds of the ten directions are offered to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Great Bodhicitta.
I now resolve my mind to make offerings with utmost sincerity and prostrate with a devoted heart until the end of the future.

**Chapter Three: The Door of Repentance** I, disciple [Name], from the beginningless past until this very day, have been afflicted by all afflictions such as greed, anger, and ignorance, as well as the secondary afflictions such as resentment and malice. These have disturbed my body and mind, leading me to commit extensively all manner of transgressions:
unwholesome physical actions, namely killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
Unwholesome verbal karma consists of false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and double-tongued speech;
unwholesome mental karma consists of greed, anger, and wrong views.

All afflictions have continued in succession from beginningless time, entangling and defiling the body and mind, causing the body, speech, and mind to commit immeasurable transgressions—such as killing one's father or mother, killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, or causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
They slandered the Triple Gem, beat and bound sentient beings,
violated the precepts and the fast, drank alcohol, and ate meat.
Such offenses as these were immeasurable, boundless, and beyond reckoning.
Today, with a sincere heart, we reveal and repent; having repented once, we shall forever sever the continuity [of these transgressions] and dare not commit them again.
We only pray that all Buddhas of the ten directions and all great Bodhisattvas will provide their empowerment and protective mindfulness, so that our karmic obstacles may be extinguished.
I prostrate with a sincere heart.

Section Four: The Gate of Taking Refuge. Disciple [Name], from this present body until I sit at the site of enlightenment, I take refuge in the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed three bodies; I take refuge in the Dharma-treasury of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna; and I take refuge in the Saṃgha of all non-regressive Bodhisattvas.
I only pray that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions will bear witness to us.
With the utmost sincerity, we prostrate.

Section Five: The Gate of Generating the Bodhicitta. Disciple [Name], from this present body until sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I vow to generate the unsurpassed, great Bodhicitta:
Sentient beings are infinite; I vow to deliver them all. Merit and wisdom are infinite;
I vow to accumulate them all. Dharma gates are infinite; I vow to study them all. Tathāgatas are infinite; I vow to serve them all.
The unsurpassed Buddha-way; I vow to realize it.

The resolve now awakened shall further distance itself from the two marks of self and phenomena, manifesting the true suchness of original enlightenment; with the wisdom of equality appearing before one, one attains skillful wisdom and becomes fully endowed with the mind of Samantabhadra.
I only pray that all Buddhas of the ten directions and all great Bodhisattvas will bear witness to us as we repent with utmost sincerity.
Chapter Six: The Gate of Questioning Regarding Obstacles and Difficulties. First, the question is asked:

If there are those who have committed any of the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya-karma*), the preceptor should not confer the precepts upon them, but should instead instruct them to perform repentance.
They must repent with utmost sincerity for seven days, fourteen days, or even up to forty-nine days, and further for as long as one year, until a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*) manifests;
if no favorable sign appears, they shall not obtain the precepts even if they receive them.
"O sons of the Buddha, from the time of your birth, have you not killed your fathers?

If there are those who have committed even minor offenses, they must confess their sins; they must certainly not conceal them, for they will receive the retribution of great sin—and this applies likewise to all such offenders."
Those who have committed no offense answer "No.
[The questioner asks: "Have you not killed your mother?
Have you not shed the blood of a Buddha?"
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not killed your preceptor?
Have you not killed your ācārya?
Have you not caused a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha?

If any among you have committed any of the seven heinous crimes mentioned above, you must confess and repent before the assembly; you must not conceal them, for you will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering.

If one relies on the Buddha’s teaching to confess and repent openly, one will certainly attain the eradication of heavy offenses, obtain a pure body, enter the wisdom of the Buddha, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
If you have not transgressed, simply answer "no.

O Sons of the Buddha: from this day forth until you sit at the seat of enlightenment, will you be able to diligently receive and uphold all the most supreme and great vows of discipline of all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas?
This is what is called the Threefold Pure Precepts:
the precept of restraining misconduct, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
From this body until you attain Buddhahood, you shall vow not to transgress them during that interval.
"Can you uphold them?
"I can," he replied.
"In the meantime, do not abandon the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) or the four great vows (*catur-mahā-praṇidhāna*)."
"Can you uphold it? "I can.

Having thus generated the bodhicitta and received the Bodhisattva precepts, we pray that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions will bear witness to us, grant us their empowerment, and cause us never to fall back.
With a sincere heart, we prostrate ourselves.

Section Seven: Inviting the Teachers and Disciples. We, the disciples such as [Name], respectfully invite all Buddhas of the ten directions and all Bodhisattvas—namely Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Bodhisattva, and all other great assemblies of Bodhisattvas—to remember their original vows and descend to this site of practice to bear witness for us.
With a sincere heart, I prostrate.

Disciple [Name], I respectfully invite Śākyamuni Buddha to be my Upādhyāya; I respectfully invite Mañjuśrī to be my Karmācārya; I respectfully invite the Buddhas of the ten directions to be my Precept-Witnessing Teachers; and I respectfully invite all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas to be my fellow practitioners of the Dharma.
I only pray that all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, will graciously accept my invitation.
I prostrate with a sincere heart.
Section Eight: The Gate of Karmavācanā. Listen attentively, O sons of the Buddha; I shall now confer the precepts upon you through the rite of karmavācanā.
This is precisely the time for receiving the precepts; listen with a sincere mind and attentively to the *karmavācanā* text:
"May all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and all great Bodhisattvas, look upon us with compassion and mindfulness."

"O sons of the Buddha, from this day forth until you sit at the seat of enlightenment, you shall receive and train in the pure precepts of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future—namely, the precept of restraining misconduct, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the precept of benefiting sentient beings. You shall fully receive and uphold these three pure precepts," thus repeating it a second and a third time.
I prostrate with a sincere heart.

Chapter Nine: The Section on Establishing the Precepts. All sons of the Buddha, from this day forth until you realize unsurpassed bodhi, you shall fully receive and uphold the pure precepts of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Now that you have received the pure precepts, you should maintain them in this manner; [repeat] thus up to three times.
With a sincere heart, pay homage with your head bowed. 10.

Cultivating the Four Means of Integration, Chapter Ten. Regarding the cultivation of the four means of integration: O Sons of the Buddha, having as previously described awakened the bodhicitta and been endowed with the bodhisattva precepts, you should now cultivate the four methods of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the ten grave precepts, and must not allow them to be deficient or violated.

As for the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), they are namely: giving (*dāna*), affectionate speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*). One should practice giving because one wishes to subdue beginningless stinginess and greed, and to bring benefit to sentient beings;
one should practice affectionate speech because one wishes to subdue the afflictions of anger and pride, and to benefit sentient beings;
one should cultivate beneficial conduct because one wishes to bring benefit to sentient beings and to fulfill one's original vows.

In order to draw near to great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and to ensure that the virtuous mind is never interrupted, one should practice these four methods of "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*); this is the locus of such cultivation.

11. The Eleventh Section on the Ten Grave Precepts. Regarding the ten grave precepts that all Buddha-sons who receive and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts must observe—namely, these ten grave precepts—I shall now proclaim them; listen with a sincere mind and attend closely.
First, one should not retreat from the bodhicitta, for that would obstruct the attainment of Buddhahood.
Second, one should not abandon refuge in the Triple Gem to take refuge in external paths, for those are false teachings.
Third, one should not slander the Three Jewels or the scriptures of the three vehicles, for such acts turn one's back on the Buddha-nature.
Fourth, regarding those points in the profound Mahāyāna sūtras that are not yet understood, one should not give rise to doubt or confusion, for they are not within the domain of ordinary beings.

Fifth, if there are sentient beings who have already resolved upon bodhicitta, one should not preach such a teaching to them, causing them to retreat from bodhicitta and turn toward the two vehicles, for this would sever the lineage of the Triple Gem.

Sixth, one should not preach such a Dharma to those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta, lest it cause them to give rise to the mind of the two vehicles, thereby contravening their original vow.

Seventh, one should not rashly preach the profound and wondrous Mahāyāna before those of the Hīnayāna or those with false views, for fear that they might give rise to slander and incur great calamity.
Eighth, one should not give rise to various views such as false views, for this would cause the severing of the roots of goodness.

Ninth, before followers of external paths, one should not say of oneself, "I possess the sublime precepts of unsurpassed bodhi," lest they, out of resentment, seek such things; if they fail to obtain them, it will cause them to retreat from the bodhicitta, resulting in harm to both parties.

Tenth: regarding all sentient beings, one should never perform, nor teach others to perform, nor rejoice in seeing performed, any act that causes harm or provides no benefit, because such acts are contrary to the dharmas for benefiting others and to the mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
The above constitutes the completion of the bestowal of the Bodhisattva precepts; you should maintain them with such purity and refrain from any violation.
Thus concludes the reception of the Threefold Pure Precepts.
Next, one should receive the profound principles of the Mahāyāna, the Dharma-gate of the Secret Essential Samādhi of Contemplative Wisdom.

Now, in wishing to receive this Dharma, one must recognize that it is profoundly abstruse and those who believe in it are exceedingly rare; therefore, it should not be bestowed before a multitude, but granted secretly after assessing the recipient's capacity.

One must first employ various skillful means to harmonize with the holy teachings, causing them to give rise to firm faith and decisively eliminate the net of doubt; only then can they be enlightened.
The Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha said:

"The faculties and dispositions of sentient beings differ, and thus the Great Sage established teachings that are likewise not uniform. One must not dogmatically cling to a single teaching and judge others as right or wrong; if one cannot even attain the rewards of humans or devas, how much less can one attain the Unsurpassed Way?"

There are those who attain Buddhahood by practicing giving alone; there are those who likewise become Buddhas by cultivating only the precepts; and through patience, diligence, meditation, wisdom, and even the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—entering each and every gate, one attains Buddhahood.
"Now, for the time being, I shall provide a skillful means based on the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* so that you may perform this practice until you attain Buddhahood.
Upon hearing these words, you should purify your own mind and dwell in tranquil composure.

Thereupon, the Tripitaka Master remained amidst the assembly without rising from his seat; he was silent and motionless as if having entered meditative concentration. After what seemed like a long time, he arose from samādhi and surveyed the fourfold assembly.
The fourfold assembly joined their palms and bowed their heads, expressing their profound respect with repeated words of farewell.
After a long time, the Tripitaka Master spoke:

"Although you previously received the bodhisattva precepts of purity, you must now again receive the internal, realized, untainted, and pure dharma-precepts of all Buddhas; only then may you enter the gate of dhyāna."
Once one has entered the gate of dhyāna, it is essential to recite this dhāraṇī.
This dhāraṇī is ultimately supreme and equal to that of all Buddhas; by mounting this vehicle, one awakens to and enters the ocean of all-knowledge—this is called the true Dharma-precept.
This Dharma is secret and must not be heard indiscriminately. If one wishes to hear it, one must first receive a *dhāraṇī*, which says:

"Oṃ samaye sattvaṃ. One should recite this *dhāraṇī* three times; only then may one hear the precepts and other secret teachings. Furthermore, one will be able to fulfill all the pure disciplinary codes (*śīla*) of the Bodhisattvas, whose great merits are beyond full description.
Furthermore, for the sake of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, he bestowed another *dhāraṇī*, saying:
"Oṃ jñidhyatamunadhyami. If this *dhāraṇī* is recited three times, one will immediately generate the bodhicitta and proceed until the attainment of Buddhahood, remaining firm and never regressing.
Furthermore, for the sake of realization and entry, he again received a dhāraṇī, which says:

"Oṃ jita-prativedi-taṅka-ru-mi. If this dhāraṇī is recited three times, one immediately attains the treasury of all profound precepts and is endowed with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), swiftly realizing unsurpassed bodhi; thus do all Buddhas speak in unison.
Furthermore, for the sake of entering the stage of Bodhisattva practice, he bestowed another dhāraṇī, saying:
“Oṃ vajramaṇḍala-praviśa me. If this dhāraṇī is recited three times, one immediately realizes the rank of all consecration maṇḍalas and attains unimpeded access to all secrets.
Having already entered the stage of the Bodhisattva’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one is fit to receive the gate of dhyāna.
Thus concludes the bestowal of the untainted true Dharma precepts.
Furthermore, as a preliminary protection for the practitioner, one shall be granted a *dhāraṇī*, which says:

"Oṃ śuddha śuddha. First, recite this one hundred thousand times to eliminate all obstacles, purify the three karmas, and extinguish the defilements of sin; thus, one will not be disturbed by demons or malevolent influences, just as pure white silk easily accepts dye.
The practitioner is likewise: once the obstacles of sin have been extinguished, they will swiftly realize samādhi."
"Furthermore, for the practitioner, I bestow a single dhāraṇī, which says:

Oṃ sarvavid svāhā. Regarding the method of recitation, whether it be the two preceding dhāraṇīs or this one, recite whichever you prefer; they must not be recited together, for I fear that the mind will lose its single-minded concentration."

"Furthermore, for one who wishes to enter samādhi, at the time of initial practice, one must sever all external objects and eliminate all distracting affairs. Having sat alone in a quiet place in the half-lotus posture, one must first perform the hand mudrā for protection: join the thumbs and wisdom fingers (tarjanī) together and extend them upright; then, with the fingers of the right hand pressing over those of the left, cross them properly so that the two backs touch; join the index fingers (agraṅgulī) together and extend them upright, touching their tips while curving them slightly, leaving a small opening at the heart; finally, join the middle fingers (madhyamā) together and extend them upright—thus it is completed."

Having formed this mudrā, first seal the crown of the head, next seal the forehead; then place the seal on the right shoulder, followed by the left shoulder, and then seal the heart. Next, place the seal on the right knee, then seal the left knee. At each location where a seal is applied, recite the aforementioned dhāraṇī seven times, continuing until all seven locations have been completed.

Thereafter, having performed the mudrā-dissolution upon the crown of the head, one should take up a rosary and recite this dhāraṇī. If one is able to recite it two hundred or three hundred times, or even as many as three thousand or five thousand times, that shall suffice.
Every time you sit for meditation, recite [the mantra] until you complete one *lakṣa* (100,000); this is the most extraordinary method of accomplishment.

Once you have consecrated your body, sit upright and straight as before, in the half-lotus posture with the right leg pressing upon the left. It is not necessary to perform the full lotus posture; for the full lotus causes much pain, and if the mind is distracted by the sensation of pain, it will be difficult to attain meditative concentration.
If one has previously mastered the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), it is most excellent.

However, one should keep the head straight and gaze level; the eyes should not be opened too wide, nor should they be completely closed. If opened too wide, the mind becomes distracted; if closed, one falls into torpor (*styāna*).
Do not rely on external objects; simply sit at ease until the session is concluded.

However, you may direct your mind toward making offerings and repentance. First, focus your mind to observe all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, who are preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly amidst the gathering of devas and humans.
Thereafter, one observes one's own body and, before each and every Buddha, reverently prostrates and offers praise with the three karmas.
When the practitioner performs this visualization, they must make it clear and distinct as if facing them directly, seeing them with extreme clarity.

Thereafter, one directs the mind toward the worlds of the ten directions, offering all manner of sublime incense, flowers, banners, canopies, food, drink, and precious jewels throughout the entirety of space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm—making offerings to all Buddhas, the great Bodhisattvas, and the Dharma, Reward, and Transformation bodies; to the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits; and to the great assemblies.

After the practitioner has performed this offering, they should then direct their mind before each of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, giving rise to a heart of profound respect and utmost sincerity, and confess as follows:

"From beginningless time until today, our afflictions have shrouded our minds as we have long wandered through birth and death; the karmic actions of our body, speech, and mind are difficult to recount in full."
I now know only how to perform extensive repentance; once this single repentance is completed, I shall forever sever the continuity [of transgressions] so that they never arise again.

I only pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, by the power of their great compassion, will bestow their majestic protection and mindfulness, and graciously accept my repentance, so that my karmic obstacles may be swiftly extinguished. This is called the inner secret repentance; it is most subtle and wondrous.
"Next, one should make the great vow:

'I have long been within the stream of existence; perhaps in the past, I practiced the bodhisattva path to bring benefit and happiness to boundless sentient beings, or cultivated meditative concentration, diligently applied myself with vigor to guard the three karmas, and accumulated merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, up to the fruit of Buddhahood.'"

I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will arouse the power of their compassionate vows, bestowing their majestic protection and mindfulness upon me, so that by means of these merits, I may swiftly accord with all gates of samādhi, swiftly accord with all gates of dhāraṇī, and swiftly attain the purity of all intrinsic natures.
Thus, one should extensively make such vows so that [the practice] does not decline or be lost, and is swiftly accomplished.
Next, one should train in the regulation of the breath (*ānāpāna*).

As for the regulation of the breath: first, one should visualize the inhalation and exhalation flowing through each and every limb, joint, tendon, and vessel within one's own body, and then exhale slowly through the mouth.

Furthermore, one should visualize this breath as white as snow and as moist and lustrous as milk; one must also know the distance it reaches, then slowly draw it back in through the nose, causing it to permeate the entire body until it completely pervades even the sinews and veins.
In this manner, perform the inhalation and exhalation three times each.

By practicing this regulation of breath, ensure that the body is free from afflictions and that cold, heat, wind, and other elements are all rendered peaceful and comfortable; only then should one train in meditative concentration.
The Tripitaka Master Śubhakara said:

"You are a beginner who fears the arising of thoughts and mental activity; if you cease your diligent pursuit and instead focus solely on maintaining non-thought as the ultimate goal, you will find that no growth is possible."
Now, there are two kinds of thought: first, unwholesome thought; second, wholesome thought.
Unwholesome and deluded thoughts must be eliminated in every respect.
Wholesome thoughts of the True Dharma must not be allowed to cease.
A true practitioner must first cultivate right mindfulness before eventually reaching ultimate purity.

It is like a person learning archery who, through long practice, becomes so proficient that no further mental effort is required; whether walking or standing, their conduct is always conjoined with meditative concentration.
Do not harbor thoughts of fear or dread; such afflictions will hinder your progress in study.
"Next, you should cultivate *samādhi*.
What is called *samādhi* is nothing other than the intrinsically pure mind of all sentient beings, which is named the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*)."
From the Buddhas above down to the most minute insects below, all are entirely equal, without increase or decrease.
It is only because they are shrouded by the adventitious dust of ignorance and delusive thought that they wander through birth and death and fail to become Buddhas.
The practitioner should settle the mind in tranquil stillness and not take any external objects as a basis for perception.

One should visualize a single, perfectly luminous orb like a pure moon, positioned four feet away from the body, directly facing the face, neither too high nor too low, measuring exactly one cubit in diameter and complete in its form. Its color is brilliant and clear, with a radiant purity both inside and out, such that nothing in the world can be compared to it.

Although it was not visible at first, after long and diligent investigation, one will eventually see it through; having done so, one should further observe it and gradually expand the scope—whether to four feet, doubling it in this manner until it fills the entire trichiliocosm, making it as distinct as possible.
When one is about to emerge from contemplation, these [visualizations] are gradually abbreviated until they return to their original state.
At the time of the initial contemplation, it is like the moon; after it has pervaded everywhere, it no longer possesses squareness or roundness.
Having performed this contemplation, one immediately realizes the samādhi of liberation from all veils and hindrances.

One who attains this samādhi is called a "worthy one" (ārya) among the three stages prior to the bhūmis; progressing gradually by means of this until pervading the entire dharma-realm is, as stated in the sūtras, called the first bhūmi.

The reason it is called the First Ground is that, by realizing this Dharma which was previously unattained and is now for the first time attained, one gives rise to great joy; therefore, the First Ground is named "Joy" (Pramuditā).
Nor should one form conceptual understandings [of it].
This very mind of intrinsic purity is like the moon for three reasons:
first, the sense of intrinsic purity, because it is free from the defilement of desire;...
Second is the meaning of coolness, because it is free from the feverish affliction of anger;
third is the meaning of radiance, because it is free from the darkness of ignorance.
Furthermore, the moon is composed of the four great elements and will ultimately perish; thus, since the moon is commonly seen by the world, it is taken as a metaphor to lead others to realization.

When the practitioner has practiced this contemplation for a long time and its cultivation is perfected, there is no need to prolong or hasten it; one perceives only luminous clarity with nothing else present, and neither body nor mind is seen.
All phenomena are unattainable, like empty space; yet do not form a conceptual understanding of them as "empty.

Because they are characterized by non-conceptualization and so forth, they are said to be like empty space, but this does not mean one should harbor the thought of emptiness. Through long-term cultivation, whether in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, at all times and in all places—whether with deliberate mental engagement or without—it will spontaneously accord with reality, free from all obstruction.
All delusive thoughts, including all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and ignorance, do not require deliberate severance; they naturally fail to arise, for their nature is eternally pure.
By practicing in reliance upon this, one attains Buddhahood; there is only this single path, and no other principle exists beyond it.
This is the path of internal realization of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is not the domain of the followers of the Two Vehicles or of external paths.

Having cultivated this contemplation, one realizes that all Buddha-dharmas and their merits, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are not awakened to through another, but are unified by means of this One, thereby attaining spontaneous penetration.

Able to open up a single syllable to expound immeasurable dharmas, one awakens and enters into all phenomena in a single kṣaṇa, attaining sovereign mastery and non-obstruction; there is no coming or going, no arising or ceasing—all are equal.
"By practicing this, one gradually reaches the signs of advancement; through long-term personal realization, these will be known, for they cannot be fully exhausted by preliminary explanation.
The Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha said:

"Once you have been able to cultivate and achieve mastery in the contemplation of oneness, you should further understand that within this mind there are five meanings of the mind, which the practitioner must know:"

The first is the momentary mind (*kṣaṇika-citta*): this refers to the initial mind that, upon seeing the Path (*darśana-mārga*), corresponds with it for a single thought-moment before quickly forgetting and losing it; like a flash of lightning at night, which appears briefly and then vanishes, it is therefore called "momentary."

The second is the "flowing-in" mind (*pravāha-citta*): having already seen the Path, one applies effort in every thought-moment in an uninterrupted succession, like a torrential stream rushing forward; hence it is called "flowing-in."

Third is the sweet and pleasant mind (*madhura-citta*): this means that by practicing merit without ceasing, one eventually attains a state of emptiness, clarity, and transparency; body and mind become light and at ease, and one relishes the flavor of the Way, hence it is called "sweet and pleasant."
Fourth is the mind that crushes and scatters: because it gives rise to diligence abruptly and then again abandons it, both states deviate from the Way;

hence it is called "crushing and scattering. Fifth is the mirror-like mind: having already departed from the distracted mind, it reflects with perfect clarity and remains unattached to anything; hence it is called the "bright mirror."
If you thoroughly understand these five minds and verify them within yourself, you will be able to distinguish for yourself the stages of the three vehicles, from ordinary beings to sages.

You practitioners who are beginners in the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) should practice the method of cultivating concentration through the secret empowerment of the skillful means of the Buddhas of the past; this is because it is identical with and corresponds to all gates of dhāraṇī. Therefore, you must receive these four dhāraṇīs.
The dhāraṇī is:
Oṃ sucakṣma vajra. According to the Chinese commentary in an alternative edition:
Oṃ sucakṣa vajra. "This dhāraṇī can cause whatever one contemplates to be accomplished."
“Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra. This dhāraṇī can ensure that what is being contemplated is not lost.”
“Oṃ sphara vajra. This dhāraṇī can cause the object of contemplation to gradually expand.”
“Oṃ saṃhāra-vajra. This dhāraṇī can cause that which is being visualized to expand, and then cause it to gradually contract back to its original state.”
"These four dhāraṇīs are the profound skillful means within the self-realized Dharma of Bhagavān, which opens the way for all practitioners to swiftly realize and enter it."

If one wishes to swiftly seek this samādhi, one should constantly recite this dhāraṇī during the four modes of conduct; by applying oneself with focused mindfulness and never allowing even a moment’s neglect, there will be no lack of swift efficacy.
"You who practice meditative concentration must also know the rules for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).

In a quiet place, level and clean ground should be prepared, twenty-five cubits in length, with markers erected at both ends and a rope stretched across the entire length, positioned just level with the chest."
He used a bamboo tube to hold the cord, which was long enough to be grasped by hand; the tube rotated to the right with the sun as it moved back and forth in a level, straight line.

With a mind that universally surveyed the space of six feet before him, he relied on the awakening of samādhi to maintain his fundamental mind, perceiving everything with clear discernment so as not to let it be lost.

Simply step down once and recite one mantra; in this manner, from the first to the last, these four mantras are repeated in a cycle from beginning to end, and one should continue reciting and contemplating them without ceasing.
If you feel even slightly weary or lax, you should immediately sit as comfortably as possible.

The practitioner should understand the skillful means for entering the Way, which deeply assists progress like the Vajra of Cultivating the Mind—unwavering and unchanging. Donning the great armor of diligence and generating a fierce and keen resolve, one should vow to achieve the goal as the appointed time, never allowing for any regression. One must not allow distracting studies to delude the mind, causing this entire life to pass in vain.

"However, the Dharma has no dual characteristics, and both mind and speech are forgotten therein. Yet, if one does not employ skillful means to reveal it, there is no way to enter its realization. This is because Sanskrit and Chinese are vastly different; were it not for translation, it would be difficult to comprehend. Having received this brief guidance, I have recorded it according to my recollection to transmit it to those who have not yet awakened."
The Chan Master Huijing of Ming Temple in the western capital previously compiled this work; I have now revised and supplemented it in detail, deeming it quite complete.
Namo! I bow my head to the Buddhas of the ten directions, To the gate of nectar within the ocean-treasury of True Suchness, And to the Sangha of the Three Sages, Ten Sages, and Arhats:
I pray that you grant your majestic power and the strength of your mindfulness.
This rare and essential secret of dharani and dhyāna, Which can give rise to the perfect, luminous, and vast mind—
I now briefly extol it according to my capacity, And dedicate the merit to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
